title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Pipelines | MPI, US
description: On-site magnetic particle inspection for US pipelines: dents, SCC colonies, sleeve and fitting welds, station piping. Mobilized to your dig. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Pipelines: Cracks, Dents and Repair Welds
html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection on United States pipelines: cracks at dents and gouges, stress corrosion cracking colonies, sleeve and fitting welds, hot-tap and branch connections, and station piping in carbon steel. Technicians are mobilized to the dig, the station or the shop yard with yokes, fluorescent and visible suspensions, and portable lighting. Send the pipe details, the feature to be checked and the governing code, and request an MT inspection quote.

Why magnetic particle inspection matters on pipe

Wall loss is measured with ultrasound, but cracking is a surface question first, and on ferromagnetic line pipe the most sensitive field method for tight surface-breaking cracks is magnetic particle inspection. Pipeline operators call for it whenever steel has been plastically deformed, welded or exposed to a cracking environment: at a dent after an in-line tool flags it, along a seam or girth weld toe, inside a patch of stress corrosion cracking, and on every new weld made during a repair. If you also need wall readings at the same excavation, our ultrasonic work on pipelines uses the same cleaned steel.

The method has a hard limit that shapes the scope: it only works on ferromagnetic material. Carbon and low-alloy line pipe qualifies. Austenitic stainless steel, many valve trims and non-ferrous components do not, and those items go to liquid penetrant testing on pipelines. We say so up front in the quote so you do not buy the wrong examination.

The regulatory and code background

Gas pipe is governed by PHMSA 49 CFR Part 192 and liquids pipe by Part 195. Both require welds to be examined to a recognized standard, and both expect repairs to be made to a method the operator can show is sound. ASME B31.8 and B31.4 supply the design and repair framework, and API 1104 covers welding of pipelines, including in-service welding on pipe that is carrying product. Acceptance of an indication is not set by the technician: it comes from the operator’s specification or the repair code, and our report quotes the criterion the operator names.

For field practice the examination is written to ASME Section V, Article 7 and the related ASTM practices, E709 as a guide to the method and E1444 for the practice. Our explainer on Article 7 magnetic particle requirements covers what a procedure must state. Technicians work under the company written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II technicians performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports.

Cracking mechanisms we look for

  • Dent and gouge cracking. Mechanical damage can leave cracks at the dent shoulder or at the base of a gouge. The pipe surface is blasted clean and examined in two field directions.
  • Stress corrosion cracking. Colonies appear as fine, parallel, axially oriented cracks in a patch of corroded steel. Wet fluorescent particles reveal them best, and the extent of the colony is mapped for the operator.
  • Seam weld defects. Older longitudinal seams may carry hook cracks, lack of fusion and selective seam corrosion that opens to the surface.
  • Girth and repair weld toes. Toe cracks, crater cracks and lack of fusion on completed repairs and on welds disturbed by pressure testing.
  • Fatigue at attachments. Cracking where supports, saddles and clamps bear on the pipe or where vibration works a branch connection.

Sizing the depth of a crack is a specialist task we do not offer on this page. If an indication is found, the operator’s engineer decides whether the feature is ground out, repaired or reassessed.

Technique in a pipeline trench

Pipeline MT is done with an AC or permanent-magnet yoke for most field work. Prods are used only where the procedure permits them, because arc strikes can create the damage we are looking for. A yoke is placed so the field is across the suspected flaw direction, then rotated 90 degrees and the area re-examined, so flaws in either orientation are seen. Lift capacity of the yoke is verified on a test block before use, and the field is checked with a gaussmeter or a field indicator where the procedure requires it.

Dry powder is useful on a warm, dry pipe, and the choice of colour follows the contrast against the cleaned steel. On pipe that is wet, cold or rough, wet suspension is used instead, and fluorescent suspension is chosen when the highest sensitivity is needed, for example on an SCC colony. Fluorescent work needs a dark environment: typically ultraviolet light of about 1,000 microwatts per square centimeter at the test surface and white-light levels in the viewing area kept very low. In a daytime trench that means a tent or hood; many operators schedule the examination around dusk or use a portable enclosure. Visible-colour wet particles need good white light instead, about 100 foot-candles at the surface.

Surface preparation is the big variable. Coating, rust and weld spatter must be removed so the particles can contact the steel, and the operator’s coating crew usually does the heavy removal. Blasting can smear metal and close fine cracks, so we ask for a final light cleaning, and we examine the surface after cleaning, not before. Pipe temperature affects the carrier fluid: below freezing a heated enclosure is the practical answer, and above the range the procedure permits, the pipe must cool.

Repair welds, sleeves and hot-tap fittings

Pipeline repairs involve welding on steel that may still be pressurized, and welds made under those conditions are examined carefully. We perform magnetic particle examination of sleeve fillet welds, saddle and branch connection welds, and the welds on split-tee fittings used for hot taps. The sequence usually goes: examine the base metal before welding, examine the root and any intermediate passes the procedure requires, and examine the completed weld after the specified wait time. Our page on magnetic particle weld inspection covers technique on welds in detail.

ASME PCC-2 and the operator’s own repair procedures set which repairs require surface examination and what is acceptable. When you send a repair drawing, we match the examination sequence to it and note which welds can only be inspected after the sleeve is installed.

Reading indications: relevant, non-relevant and false

Not every particle build-up is a crack. Magnetic writing from a nearby magnetized object, a sharp change in section, a scratch or a weld-ripple edge can hold powder without a flaw underneath. The technician classifies each indication as relevant, non-relevant or false, and says how. A common test is to wipe the indication clean, re-apply the particles in a different field direction, and see whether it returns in the same place with the same shape. Cracks usually reappear sharp and continuous; scratches and ripple edges do not. When doubt remains, the area is lightly dressed and re-examined, or the operator is told the indication cannot be classified.

Residual magnetism matters on pipe that has been handled with magnetic lifting equipment or that sits near cathodic protection rectifiers and welding returns. Where it interferes, the yoke field is applied in opposite polarities and the technician notes the effect in the report. This kind of detail is why the procedure and the Level III review exist, and why a plain photograph of powder on a pipe is not an inspection record.

Where MT is the wrong choice

Typical pipeline items and the method we recommend
ItemRecommended methodReason
Carbon steel dent or gougeMT, wet fluorescent where possibleFinds tight surface cracks quickly over a wide area
Stainless or nickel alloy station tubingPTNot ferromagnetic, so particles will not form indications
Wall thickness under a corrosion patchUTMT shows surface cracks only, not remaining wall
Embedded lack of fusion in a thick sleeve weldUT angle beamMT sees only flaws open to or just below the surface
Painted or heavily coated pipeRemove coating, then MTThick coatings weaken the leakage field and hide fine cracks

What the report contains

  • Operator, line or station, component or dig number, and the location tied to a clock position and a weld or marker dimension.
  • Pipe grade, diameter and wall, and the surface condition after cleaning.
  • Procedure number, revision and the code it was written to.
  • Equipment: yoke model and the lift check, particles, carrier, lamp readings for fluorescent work, and the field directions used.
  • Technician, SNT-TC-1A level and the reviewing Level III.
  • Indications with position, length and orientation, with a photograph or sketch, and the criterion applied when the operator provides one.
  • A statement of what was not examined and why, such as areas under a sleeve or an inaccessible clock position.

What to send for a quote

  1. Pipe diameter, wall, grade and operating pressure range for the lines concerned.
  2. The list of features: dents, gouges, welds, SCC patches, fittings, with locations.
  3. Code, edition and the operator’s procedure or repair specification.
  4. Who will clean the steel and what coating is present.
  5. Whether work will be at night or in an enclosure, plus access and permit constraints.
  6. Badging, site orientation and operator qualification requirements.

Planning on US pipeline projects

Pipeline work moves with weather and contractor sequences. We ask for the dig schedule so we can mobilize once the steel is exposed and cleaned. Open trenches need shoring and gas monitoring; stations need hot-work permits and lockout. Fluorescent examinations are scheduled around enclosure setup, and cold-weather work in the northern plains and mountain states needs warm enclosures for suspension and instruments. Rain and snow in an open trench make dry powder impractical, so we bring wet materials as a fallback. We follow site rules and stop work when conditions fall outside the procedure.

Where we work in the United States

  • Houston: Gulf Coast transmission, terminal and station piping with repair work around refinery corridors.
  • Tulsa: mid-continent liquids lines with long-running dent and seam programs.
  • Midland: Permian gathering lines where sour service raises cracking concern.
  • Oklahoma City: Anadarko gathering and compressor stations with welded repairs.
  • Kansas City: interstate gas lines with older seam welds.
  • Denver: Rockies gathering systems and cold-weather digging.
  • Shreveport: Haynesville gas lines at higher pressure.
  • Pittsburgh: Appalachian midstream lines on steep right-of-way.
  • Omaha: Midwest transmission and liquids lines near river crossings.

What we do not do

We do not perform radiography in the United States, we do not run in-line tools, and we do not calculate remaining life or reassessment intervals. We also do not offer crack depth sizing, and we do not present MT as a wall-thickness method. See pipeline inspection services for the broader scope and MT versus PT compared for method selection.

Training your own technicians

Operators building an in-house crew can use MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with simulator practice for magnetic particle testing, and the pipeline NDT training national page. The employer certifies its own people under its written practice, which we can help you draft.

faq.q: Can you find stress corrosion cracking with magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Yes, on carbon steel line pipe. Wet fluorescent particles under ultraviolet light reveal fine, axially aligned crack colonies after the coating is removed and the steel is cleaned. The operator’s engineer decides what to do with the colony.

faq.q: Does MT work on stainless steel station piping?
faq.a: No. Austenitic stainless steel is not ferromagnetic, so the particles cannot form indications. For stainless tubing, valve bodies and non-magnetic fittings we use liquid penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: Which codes drive pipeline magnetic particle examination?
faq.a: PHMSA 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 set the regulatory framework, with ASME B31.8, ASME B31.4 and API 1104 supplying design, repair and welding requirements. The examination itself follows ASME Section V, Article 7 and the operator’s written procedure.

faq.q: Who decides if a crack indication is rejectable?
faq.a: The operator does, through its engineer or qualified inspector, using the specification or repair code it names. We report the indication, its location and size, and quote the criterion supplied.

faq.q: Can MT be done on coated pipe?
faq.a: Heavy coating weakens the leakage field and hides fine cracks, so the coating is removed at the examination area first. Thin non-conductive coatings may be allowed by a qualified procedure, but we check that with the operator before the dig.

faq.q: Do you inspect welds on pressurized pipe?
faq.a: We examine sleeve, saddle and fitting welds made under the operator’s in-service welding procedure, following its sequence and wait times. Decisions about welding on live pipe belong to the operator.

faq.q: Why is fluorescent work scheduled differently?
faq.a: Ultraviolet indications need a dark viewing area, so we use a tent or hood in daylight or schedule the examination near dusk. The enclosure also protects the suspension from wind, rain and cold.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a pipeline MT job?
faq.a: Pipe size, wall, grade, the feature list with locations, the governing code and procedure, who will clean the steel, coating type, access and permit conditions, and the site address.

faq.q: Do you perform radiography on pipeline welds?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC or Agreement State rules. We can support with magnetic particle, penetrant and ultrasonic work and with Level III review of your procedures.
